title: A Post at the River Mouth: Singapore, 1819
setting: Singapore island and the Johor Sultanate, January–February 1819, with an epilogue in 1823
description: You are a junior interpreter attached to Stamford Raffles' expedition. Over three stages you help negotiate a British trading post at Singapore: first with the Temenggong who governs the island, then with the rival claimants to the Johor throne, and finally with Resident Farquhar over how the new settlement should be run. Each decision is resolved against what the stakeholders actually want, and the debrief compares your path with what really happened.
learningObjectives: Explain why the East India Company wanted a port at the southern end of the Straits of Malacca
Describe the disputed Johor succession and why Raffles recognised Tengku Hussein
Evaluate the risks each stakeholder took in signing the 1819 agreements
Distinguish documented history from simulated assumptions in the adventure

player.name: Ahmad bin Yusof
player.role: Junior interpreter to the East India Company expedition
player.brief: You speak Malay and English and have been attached to Raffles' party as an interpreter. You carry messages, sit in on negotiations and are trusted by neither side completely. Your recommendations shape what Raffles and Farquhar decide, but the Temenggong and the Johor princes have their own plans.

sources.title: The Founding of a Trading Post at Singapore, 1819 (classroom handout)

sharedContext.text: It is January 1819. The Dutch have returned to Java and Malacca and are extending their authority over Riau. British merchants trading with China want a safe harbour of their own at the southern end of the Straits of Malacca. Stamford Raffles, Lieutenant-Governor of Bencoolen, has permission from Lord Hastings in Calcutta to look for a site, but he has been told to avoid any collision with the Dutch. He has sailed from Penang with Major William Farquhar and a small squadron. Singapore is part of the Johor Sultanate and is administered by the Temenggong, Abdul Rahman. The Johor throne is disputed between two brothers.

spans.quote: British merchants trading with China complained that they had no safe harbour of their own at the southern end of the Straits of Malacca.
he was to establish a post at the southern end of the Straits but to avoid any collision with the Dutch, who were then extending their authority over Riau.
The island was administered on the Sultan's behalf by the Temenggong, Abdul Rahman

assumptions.text: The player character, a junior Malay–English interpreter named Ahmad bin Yusof, is invented. No such named person appears in the source.
assumptions.rationale: The student needs a role that can plausibly be present at every negotiation without displacing a documented actor.

assumptions.text: The private motivations, fears and hidden interests attributed to each stakeholder are dramatised inferences from their documented actions, not quotations from the record.
assumptions.rationale: The handout records what each person did, not what they privately thought; the simulation needs motives to make agents act consistently.

assumptions.text: The specific rooms — the ship's cabin, the Temenggong's hall, Farquhar's tent, the treaty ground and the Resident's office — are schematic stand-ins for places that existed in some form but are not described in the source.
assumptions.rationale: The map needs concrete spaces; their layout is invented by the compiler.

assumptions.text: Endings other than the historical one describe what might plausibly have followed a different decision; they are counterfactual and are labelled as such in the debrief.
assumptions.rationale: The simulation must resolve every branch, but only one branch actually happened.

stakeholders.name: Sir Thomas Stamford Raffles
stakeholders.role: Lieutenant-Governor of Bencoolen, agent of the East India Company

summary.text: Raffles argued that the Company needed a station commanding the entrance to the China Sea and obtained cautious permission from Lord Hastings to find one. He arrived off Singapore on 28 January 1819 and left on 7 February, having signed a treaty and appointed Farquhar as Resident.

stakeholders.name: Major William Farquhar
stakeholders.role: Former Resident of Malacca; first Resident and Commandant of Singapore

summary.text: Farquhar had been Resident of Malacca until it was returned to the Dutch. He accompanied Raffles, was appointed to command the new settlement, and governed it from 1819 to 1823 by licensing gambling houses and tolerating the opium, arrack and slave trades to raise money — measures Raffles later condemned.

spans.quote: Major William Farquhar, who had been the Resident of Malacca until it was returned to the Dutch, accompanied him
To raise money he licensed gambling houses and permitted the sale of opium and arrack

stakeholders.name: Temenggong Abdul Rahman
stakeholders.role: Administrator of Singapore on behalf of the Sultan of Johor

summary.text: The Temenggong governed Singapore for the Johor Sultanate, having moved there with his followers a few years earlier. He signed a preliminary agreement with Raffles on 30 January 1819 and the treaty of 6 February, under which he was to receive 3,000 Spanish dollars a year.

spans.quote: On 30 January 1819 Raffles and the Temenggong signed a preliminary agreement
the Temenggong 3,000 Spanish dollars a year

stakeholders.name: Tengku Hussein (Tengku Long)
stakeholders.role: Elder son of Sultan Mahmud Shah III; recognised by Raffles as Sultan Hussein Shah of Johor

summary.text: Hussein was away in Pahang when his father died in 1812 and was passed over for his younger brother, who had Bugis and later Dutch backing. Living in obscurity in Riau, he was sent for by the Temenggong, arrived in early February 1819, and was recognised by Raffles as Sultan in return for 5,000 Spanish dollars a year.

spans.quote: The elder, Tengku Hussein, also known as Tengku Long, was away in Pahang for his wedding when his father died.

sharedContext.text: 29–30 January 1819. Raffles has landed near the mouth of the Singapore River. The island holds perhaps a thousand people. The Temenggong governs it for the Sultan of Johor, but he is not the sovereign. Raffles wants an agreement quickly; his instructions tell him to avoid a collision with the Dutch.

His younger brother Abdul Rahman sits on the throne with Bugis backing and Dutch recognition. Raffles must decide whose signature makes a treaty lawful.

sharedContext.text: 1822. Raffles has returned to find Singapore growing faster than anyone expected under Farquhar. It is a free port. Farquhar has raised money by licensing gambling houses and permitting the opium and arrack trades, and has not stopped the slave trade passing through the port. The Dutch protest continues and London has not yet decided whether to keep the settlement.

spans.quote: Raffles had declared Singapore a free port, where ships could trade without paying duties
he did not stop the trade in slaves that passed through the port
For several years it was uncertain whether the British government in London would keep the settlement.

endings.title: A free port under new management
endings.summary: Raffles redraws the town plan, ends the licensed gambling, and dismisses Farquhar, who leaves under protest. Singapore remains a free port and keeps growing.

historicalOutcome.text: This is what happened. Raffles disapproved of Farquhar's measures, redrew the town plan and in 1823 dismissed him, replacing him with John Crawfurd. The Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 ended the Dutch objection, and the January 1824 census recorded 10,683 people.

spans.quote: in 1823 dismissed Farquhar, replacing him with John Crawfurd
The dispute was finally settled by the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824

endings.divergence: Your path matches the documented outcome. The details of the conversations and the reasons the agents gave you were simulated.
reflectionQuestions: Farquhar's licences paid for the settlement. Was Raffles right to condemn them?
Why might a free port have grown faster than one that charged duties?
Which of the private motives you uncovered were documented, and which were the simulation's assumptions?

endings.title: Duties at the river mouth
endings.summary: Port duties are introduced and Farquhar stays. Some traders move their business to ports that charge nothing, and the settlement grows more slowly than it might have.

historicalOutcome.text: In reality Singapore remained a free port and traders from the region moved their business there; by January 1824 the population was 10,683. Farquhar was dismissed in 1823.

spans.quote: traders from the region moved their business there
in 1823 dismissed Farquhar

endings.divergence: Historically no duties were levied. The slower growth in this ending is a simulated consequence, not a documented one.
reflectionQuestions: What evidence in the handout suggests the free port policy mattered to Singapore's growth?
Was there a fair way to pay for the settlement without the trades Farquhar licensed?

endings.title: Refused at Riau
endings.summary: Raffles' envoy to Sultan Abdul Rahman is turned away under Dutch pressure. With no lawful grant and his sailing date past, Raffles leaves without a treaty, and the Dutch consolidate their hold on the straits.

historicalOutcome.text: Historically Raffles did not approach Sultan Abdul Rahman. He recognised Tengku Hussein and signed the treaty of 6 February 1819; the Dutch protested but withdrew their objection in the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824.

spans.quote: On 6 February 1819 a treaty was signed between the East India Company, represented by Raffles, Sultan Hussein and Temenggong Abdul Rahman.
The Dutch protested at once.

endings.divergence: This ending is counterfactual. The refusal at Riau is a simulated assumption about how a Dutch-backed Sultan would have responded.
reflectionQuestions: Why did Raffles treat the succession dispute as an opportunity rather than an obstacle?
What would the Dutch have gained if no British post had been founded in 1819?

endings.title: The flag without a treaty
endings.summary: The sepoys land and the flag is raised without any agreement. The Temenggong withdraws his welcome, the Dutch lodge a formal protest, and Calcutta, reminded of its own cautious instructions, orders the post abandoned.

historicalOutcome.text: Historically Raffles secured agreements first: a preliminary agreement with the Temenggong on 30 January and the treaty of 6 February 1819. His instructions had told him to avoid any collision with the Dutch.

spans.quote: On 30 January 1819 Raffles and the Temenggong signed a preliminary agreement
to avoid any collision with the Dutch

endings.divergence: This ending is counterfactual. Calcutta's reaction is a simulated assumption drawn from the cautious instructions in the source.
reflectionQuestions: Why did Raffles bother with agreements at all if the Company had the military power to land?
How did Raffles' cautious instructions from Calcutta shape what was possible?
